title: Neural population dynamics and temporal context cells in macaque medial parietal cortex support temporal order memory
experiments_summary: Three male rhesus macaques underwent chronic multi-unit recordings (32-channel semi-chronic Microdrive systems) from the medial posterior parietal cortex (precuneus/mPPC) while performing a temporal order judgment (TOJ) task. In the main experiment (Monkeys Jupiter and Mercury, 676 neurons across 63 sessions), monkeys watched 8-second naturalistic videos and then selected which of two probe frames appeared earlier. Two conditions were used: an immediate condition (frames 5 vs. 90) and a delayed condition (frames 95 vs. 180), with fixed temporal distances to equate temporal separation and similarity across conditions. A third monkey (Mars, Experiment 2, 198 neurons, 21 sessions) performed the same task with gaze-based responses and simultaneous eye-tracking to control for oculomotor confounds; stimuli consisted of two 4-second video clips. Neuronal classification used a Poisson GLM with stepwise selection, including regressors for block number, reaction time, trial outcome, task condition, response side, and binary epoch indicators. The TOJ epoch was decomposed into early visual-onset (0–200 ms post-probe), post-onset retrieval/comparison (200 ms post-probe to 200 ms pre-response), and response-locked motor (−200 ms to response) windows to dissociate sensory, mnemonic, and motor contributions. Reaction times were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models. Population-level spike-train synchrony was quantified using the SPIKE-distance metric across all neuron pairs within sessions, aligned to TOJ onset and response offset, with correctness and condition comparisons assessed via permutation testing with FDR correction. Temporal context cells were identified by fitting each neuron's encoding-period firing rate with three nested models (constant, Gaussian, ex-Gaussian) using likelihood ratio tests, requiring a significant ex-Gaussian fit, a minimum 2 Hz firing rate change, and a peak of at least 4 Hz. Temporal decoding of elapsed time during encoding was performed using linear discriminant analysis (LDA) with stratified 5-fold cross-validation on population firing rate vectors in 250 ms bins, with significance assessed via permutation tests; robustness was tested by progressively excluding early encoding bins. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) was conducted by computing pairwise Pearson correlations between z-scored population activity vectors in 250 ms bins across the encoding period to characterize representational drift. Encoding–retrieval similarity was quantified trial-wise using Mahalanobis distance between population firing rate vectors during encoding and TOJ periods, normalized by neuron count, with permutation controls to assess above-chance reinstatement. A linear mixed-effects model tested whether encoding–retrieval similarity depended on correctness, video half (first vs. second 4 seconds), delay condition, and their interactions. For Experiment 2, the Poisson GLM was extended with eye-movement regressors (saccade frequency, fixation frequency, total scan-path length, total fixation duration) to assess whether TOJ-related activity survived oculomotor control. Spike sorting was performed offline using the Standard E-M algorithm with quality metrics including signal-to-noise ratio, L-ratio, and isolation distance. Eye position was tracked at 1000 Hz using an infrared EyeLink 1000 Plus system.
